name: Volume eating
lead: Volume eating is the practice of building meals around low-energy-density foods, such as vegetables, fruit and broth-based soups, that supply a lot of food by weight or volume for relatively few calories, with the aim of feeling full while eating less energy [1]. It is closely related to the energy-density research of nutrition scientist Barbara Rolls, whose laboratory studies from 1998 onward examined how the calories-per-gram of foods affects how much energy people eat [8].

People use it to look leaner. A lower calorie intake with satisfying meal size supports fat loss, which reveals more of the jawline, cheekbones and muscle definition that appearance-focused communities care about; calorie restriction in general is described as producing weight and fat loss [11]. A US Centers for Disease Control report notes that because fruits and vegetables have few calories relative to volume, eating them as part of a reduced-calorie diet can be beneficial for weight management [1].

Research on the underlying principle is substantial: controlled feeding studies, a one-year randomised trial and population analyses have looked at energy density and intake [8]. Research on volume eating as a named looksmaxxing practice is limited, and the term also has unrelated meanings in bariatric and psychiatric literature, described below [2][3][4].

paras: The approach emphasises foods with few calories per unit of weight. A US Centers for Disease Control report describes fruits and vegetables as low in energy density and associated with decreased risk of chronic disease [1]. Because water and fibre add bulk without many calories, practitioners build plates around salad, cooked vegetables, fruit and soups and then add protein.

The idea is that stomach distension and meal size contribute to feeling full, so a person can eat a large-looking meal while staying within a calorie target. Wikipedia describes satiety as the fullness that follows a meal, partly signalled when stretch receptors in the stomach respond to distension and send signals to the hypothalamus via the vagus nerve [10].

In a 2023 Hacker News thread on the topic, one commenter summarised it as eating bulky, nutrient-dense, low-calorie foods so that you feel full on fewer calories, while another argued that no hack is needed and that weight loss comes down to restricting calories [5].

Laboratory work by Rolls and colleagues found that lowering the energy density of foods lowered energy intake. In a 1998 within-subject study of 18 normal-weight women, intake weight was similar across conditions, but energy intake was higher with high-energy-density entrees (about 1,800 kcal versus about 1,376 kcal), with hunger and fullness ratings that did not differ [8]. A 1999 study of lean and obese women found intake of self-selected foods about 16 percent lower on a low-density diet, and fat content of the manipulated foods had no significant effect [8].

A 2006 crossover study of 24 women reported that cutting portion size by 25 percent lowered intake by about 10 percent, while cutting energy density by 25 percent lowered intake by about 24 percent, effects that were additive, with hunger and fullness not differing significantly [8]. A 2006 cross-sectional analysis of 7,356 US adults reported lower-density diets were associated with lower energy intake and, on average, normal-weight status [8].

The year-long randomised trial of 97 obese women compared two weight-loss diets; the group told to cut fat and add fruits and vegetables ate more food by weight, reported less hunger and lost 7.9 kg versus 6.4 kg, with 71 participants completing a year [8]. Reviews by the group state that lowering energy density can reduce energy intake without reducing food volume, which may help people avoid feeling deprived [8].

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities the practice is a tactic for sustaining a cut: people describe large vegetable-heavy meals, fruit, soups and high-protein low-calorie foods to stay full while in a deficit. The wiki's focus is the appearance payoff: lower body fat is discussed as sharpening facial contours and muscle definition. Calorie restriction itself is described by Wikipedia as an intake below energy needs that produces weight and fat loss, with possible risks such as cold sensitivity, hormonal changes and, if nutrients are lacking, malnutrition [11].

The related social-media phenomenon of mukbang, eating-broadcast videos that began on AfreecaTV in 2009 and spread internationally from the mid-2010s, shows audience interest in big portions; Wikipedia reports concerns about links between problematic viewing and eating disorders [9]. A 2026 case study of an Indian mukbang creator who also produces fitness content describes vicarious gratification and appetite regulation among audiences [7].

The CDC statement describes eating fruits and vegetables within a reduced-calorie diet as beneficial for weight management [1]. The Rolls studies above examine energy density as a diet property [8]. No trial has tested volume eating as a named method for facial or body appearance outcomes.

In bariatric surgery literature, volume eating refers to eating large quantities after surgery and is cited as a cause of insufficient weight loss or weight regain after sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass. One series of repeat sleeve gastrectomy versus duodenal switch cases cites volume-eating habits as the reason for insufficient loss, and a gastric bypass series describes weight regain from new volume eating because of impaired restriction [2][3]. A 2025 paper proposes a 'volume addiction' phenotype within compulsive high-volume eating, in which patients feel an urgent drive to be profoundly full, sometimes through large volumes of low-calorie foods or fluids, and notes this is not recognised in DSM or ICD [4]. A 2026 psychiatry paper describes a fullness-seeking phenotype that overlaps binge eating disorder and food addiction [6]. These uses differ from the dieting strategy described here.

Papers on compulsive high-volume eating describe distress and weight regain in a subset of patients who pursue fullness as such [4][6]. Wikipedia notes that calorie restriction without adequate nutrients can lead to harm, and that moderate restriction may be a concern for lean people [11].

No studies found of volume eating as a looksmaxxing practice. Related research includes controlled feeding studies, a one-year trial and a national dietary analysis on energy density and intake [8], a CDC report on adult fruit and vegetable consumption in 2005 [1], and bariatric studies describing volume eating as a pattern linked to regain [2][3].

timeline.event: Rolls and colleagues report that energy density of entrees affected energy intake in normal-weight women [8].
Study finds energy density, not fat content, affected intake in lean and obese women [8].
Crossover study reports portion-size and energy-density reductions have additive effects on intake [8].
One-year randomised trial compares two weight-loss diets differing in energy density [8]; CDC reports adult fruit and vegetable consumption for 2005 [1].

lore.intro: Volume eating is discussed in fat-loss communities, for example on Hacker News in 2023, as a dieting tactic for staying full on fewer calories [5].

claims.claim: Filling meals with bulky low-calorie foods makes dieting easier.
claims.believers: Proponents say large vegetable-heavy meals keep them full while cutting calories [5].
claims.experts: The CDC notes low-energy-density foods in a reduced-calorie diet can benefit weight management, and Rolls-group trials found lower-density diets reduced intake with similar hunger ratings, while commenters in the same thread argue calorie restriction is what matters [1][8][5].

claims.claim: Eating more food by weight means eating less energy.
claims.believers: Users describe eating pounds of vegetables and fruit while staying in a deficit [5].
claims.experts: In a one-year trial, the lower-density diet group ate more food by weight, reported less hunger and lost more weight, though both groups lost weight [8].

claims.claim: Stretching the stomach is what makes it work.
claims.believers: Proponents point to stomach distension as the source of fullness.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says gastric stretch receptors contribute to satiety signalling, and Rolls-group studies measured intake and fullness ratings rather than stomach volume [10][8].

claims.claim: Chasing fullness with huge volumes can become a problem.
claims.believers: Some patients describe an urgent drive to feel profoundly full [4].
claims.experts: Psychiatric and bariatric papers describe compulsive high-volume eating and post-surgery volume eating as patterns linked to weight regain and distress [2][3][4][6].

claims.claim: No hack is needed; weight loss is calorie restriction.
claims.believers: One Hacker News commenter said you only need to restrict calories [5].
claims.experts: Calorie restriction is described as producing weight and fat loss; energy-density studies describe diet composition as one way to reduce intake [11][8].

card.summary: Filling meals with low-calorie-density foods to stay full on fewer calories; plausible for dieting but unstudied as a looksmaxxing method.
card.note: The term also describes post-surgery overeating and a compulsive-eating pattern in medical papers.

quick.overview:
Volume eating means choosing foods that give lots of bulk for few calories, such as vegetables and fruit, to feel full while dieting.

It is discussed in fat-loss circles. Source material specific to it is limited.
quick.mechanism: Low-energy-density foods supply fewer calories relative to volume, so a reduced-calorie diet built from them is described as beneficial for weight management.
quick.risks: No direct harms reported for the dieting strategy in the sources. The same term describes compulsive large-volume eating in psychiatric and bariatric papers.

chain: Meals built from bulky, low-calorie foods
Easier calorie deficit and fat loss, leaner look
angle.text: Volume eating is a way to sustain a calorie deficit while feeling full, so it supports fat loss rather than changing appearance on its own. Leaner facial and body fat is what people describe as the visible result.
